{{Short description|Theory of trace monoids}}
{{hatnote|For trace theory in natural language syntax, see [[Trace (linguistics)]].}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[computer science]], '''trace theory''' aims to provide a concrete mathematical underpinning for the study of [[concurrent computation]] and [[process calculi]]. The underpinning is provided by an [[abstract algebra|algebraic]] definition of the [[free partially commutative monoid]] or [[trace monoid]], or equivalently, the [[history monoid]], which provides a concrete algebraic foundation, analogous to the way that the [[free monoid]] provides the underpinning for [[formal language]]s.

The power of trace theory stems from the fact that the algebra of [[dependency graph]]s (such as [[Petri net]]s) is [[isomorphic]] to that of trace monoids, and thus, one can apply both algebraic [[formal language]] tools, as well as tools from [[graph theory]]. 

While the trace monoid had been studied by [[Pierre_Cartier_(mathematician)|Pierre Cartier]] and [[Dominique Foata]] for its [[combinatorics]] in the 1960s, trace theory was first formulated by [[:pl:Antoni Mazurkiewicz (informatyk)|Antoni Mazurkiewicz]] in the 1970s, in an attempt to evade some of the problems in the theory of concurrent computation, including the problems of interleaving and non-deterministic choice with regard to refinement in process calculi.
